Regarding the mathematic functions like exp, tanh and etc, TorchInductor runs into C++ std function now. Its performance is much worse than aten::vec because aten::vec leverages Sleef functions.
We have submitted a PR to establish the infrastructure - #87068. Besides that, we need to implement more features as follows.

 Support reduction
 Vectorize the tail loop with aten::vec
 Lower angle, acos, asin, atan, atan2, erfc, erfinv, expm1, log10, frac, sinh, cosh, hypot, igamma, igammac, nextafter, tan
 round, log2, log1p: couldn't find symbolic meta function/decomposition
 Support BF16
 Optimize the loop condition and loop index calculation by replacing div with add

Alternatives
To use OMP SIMD to vectorize the kernel. But it is hard to force the SIMD to run into the Sleef function to get better performance.

🐛 Describe the bug
It seems like Quantization Aware Training with Torch>=10.2 does not support nn.Embedding layers. The following example code:
class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.embed = nn.Embedding(100,100)
    
    def forward(self,x):
        return self.embed(x)
    
model = Model()

model.train()
model.qconfig = torch.quantization.get_default_qat_qconfig('fbgemm')
model = torch.quantization.prepare_qat(model)

torch.quantization.convert(model)
Runs into the following error:
torch/nn/quantized/modules/embedding_ops.py:162, in Embedding.from_float(cls, mod)
    160 dtype = weight_observer.dtype
    161 is_float_qparams_qconfig = weight_observer.qscheme == torch.per_channel_affine_float_qparams
--> 162 assert is_float_qparams_qconfig, \
    163     'Embedding quantization is only supported with float_qparams_weight_only_qconfig.'
    165 assert dtype == torch.quint8 or dtype == torch.quint4x2, \
    166     f'The only supported dtype for nnq.Embedding is torch.quint8 and torch.quint4x2, got {dtype}'
    168 # Run the observer to calculate qparams.

AssertionError: Embedding quantization is only supported with float_qparams_weight_only_qconfig.
Issues #41396 and #65185 offer solutions for static and dynamic quantization but not for quantization aware training. Is there any solution to this? If not, fixing this issue would be interesting for applications in transformers among others.

Currently, we separately allocate tensors for each invocation of cudagraphs. Especially for cases with numerous graph breaks, this can lead to a lot of wasted space. We should use a memory pool and share storage across invocations.
For HF Big Bird, implementing this was shown to improve the memory compression ratio from .96 -> 1.05. When there are more dynamic inputs and recompilations separately allocating inputs will be even more wasteful.
WIP PR: pytorch/torchdynamo#1679

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
For my use-case, I would like a certain operation to be done any time that an operation is done on a Tensor instance (e.g., save a copy of the Tensor somewhere). This is easy to do for Tensor subclasses by defining __torch_function__ and adding extra code around each function call. However, I do not see a way of doing this for the Tensor base class. This is no problem when dealing with just my own code, but I am looking to write some functionality that works for any arbitrary PyTorch model that someone might write, without changing any of the internal code of the model. For example, if inside the model someone initializes a new Tensor with torch.ones, then adds it to another tensor, then passes it through a ReLU, etc., I'd like for the Tensor to be saved after each operation (and obviously since it's someone else's model, I cannot guarantee that they use my special subclass rather than the Tensor base class; it seems like such functionality would have to be added to the Tensor class itself).
Is this at all possible, and if not, would it be easy to extend the __torch_function__ functionality (allowing arbitrary decorating of torch functions) to include not just Tensor subclasses, but the Tensor class itself? I understand this is not to be done lightly and is not necessarily "good" coding style. I am asking if it can be done, not whether it should. It's also almost certain that I'm misunderstanding some of the inner logic somewhere...
Alternatives
No response
Additional context
This works:
import torch


class MutantTensor(torch.Tensor):
    @classmethod
    def __torch_function__(cls, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
        func_output = super().__torch_function__(func, types, args, kwargs)
        print("Something is being done with a tensor.")
        return func_output


t = MutantTensor(torch.ones(5, 5))
x = t + 1
y = x * 2

Something is being done with a tensor.
Something is being done with a tensor.

import torch

old_torch_function = torch.Tensor.__torch_function__

@classmethod
def new_torch_function(cls, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
    print("Something is being done with a tensor.")
    func_output = old_torch_function(func, types, args, kwargs)
    return func_output

torch.Tensor.__torch_function__ = new_torch_function

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
I need to free some CUDA tensors (e.g., tensor a as the model parameters) to avoid OOM on GPU during the model forward. I have tried del a and call torch.cuda.empty_cache() t free both a and PyTorch GPU cache. However, the del a does not free the underlying GPU memory. The ORT is in the process of increasing coverage for the ONNX spec, and there are quite a few ops/types it doesn't support. An example is Ceil on float64.
This causes us needing to skip many different combinations of tests #86182.
Since the purpose of the tests are to ensure ONNX spec conformance, we can consider using the ONNX reference runtime, which is supposed to be better covered on the ONNX spec.
The reference runtime is implemented with numpy, which doesn't support bfloat16. So does not ORT's CPU execution provider so I think we are good there.
